The applicants' reliance on the [LOCATION] judgment was misconceived as the only power of the CMAC was to enquire as to whether the convictions were unsafe. It noted that the time for having regard to the provisions of the Convention had not yet been reached, but it was difficult to see, even in such circumstances, how provisions of Article 6 could be of any assistance.

Lord Justice [PERSON] concluded that disenfranchisement does impair the essence of a prisoner's right to vote. He said that Parliament has taken the view that for the period during which they are in custody convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote, he said. He added that Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like [Person] in [LOCATION] I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection, so the courts must afford some leeway to the legislator. The European Court also requires that the means employed to restrict the implied Convention rights to vote are not disproportionate.

The Social Insurance Office considered that the applicant’s ability to work was not reduced due to her back problems to such an extent that she was entitled to the benefits in question. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of [LOCATION]. She maintained that the medical evidence, on which the Office’s decision was based, in fact showed that she was entitled to the benefits sought. In support of her appeal she invoked medical certificates issued by three other physicians. Furthermore, without stating any reasons for her request, she asked the court to hold an oral hearing. On [DATE_TIME] the appellate court rejected the applicant's appeal. The applicant was on sick-leave during which period she received per diem sickness benefits under the Social Insurance Act (Lagen om allmän försäkring, 1962:381; hereinafter ‘the 1962 Act’). However, by a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Office found that she was no longer entitled to such benefits. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Social Insurance Court. She also complained about the lack of oral hearings in the lower courts. The Supreme Social Insurance Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. She was given the opportunity to submit further observations on the question of leave to appealed. The case appeared to be unnecessary, the court said. The application was dismissed on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements for an appeal to be heard. The court said it would consider the application again in due course. The appeal was rejected on the basis that the case was unnecessary.
